newsitem.title: USA: US OPTIONS FOCUS/Stock index vols up, calls bid.
newsitem.headline: US OPTIONS FOCUS/Stock index vols up, calls bid.

text.p: Implied volatilities for U.S. stock index options were up slightly as the stock market's bounce this week, after last Friday's selloff, fueled out-of-the-money call buying again, traders said.
As the stock market climbed into new territory, both actual and implied volatilities have been on the rise, they added.

"At these levels (in stocks), we're not going to see narrow ranges very often," said Jack Callahan, an independent market-maker in the Chicago Board Options Exchange (CBOE) S&P 100 index .OEX options pit.
"We're seeing more broad ranges and intraday swings, so option premiums should more and more reflect that," he added.
He said good risk-reward tradeoff in out-of-the-money calls during the market's run up in recent months was drawing persistent bid in those options, pushing up volatilities.
CBOE volatility index .VIX, which reflects implied volatility levels of near-month OEX options, was up 0.25 point at 24.51 at 1130 CDT/1630 GMT.
The August 930 to 950 calls, as well as the at-the-money 920 calls, were the most heavily traded OEX options, with turnover of more than 2,000 contracts each by 1130 CDT.
Put-side activity was more scattered, with 1,000-1,500 contracts trading at several strike levels.

The OEX was up 5.16 points at 919.90, slightly off early highs. Traders said the market had calmed down somewhat after Tuesday's big late rally on Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's middle-of-the-road comments in his semi-annual Humphrey-Hawkins testimony.

Jerry Hegarty, equity analyst with Thomson Research, said that even though premiums have been pumped up to high levels and he anticipated a period of relatively mixed trading in the coming weeks, he would be reluctant to sell options now.
"You can say option premiums are outrageous," he said. "On the other hand, I'm not sure the (actual) volatility's even more outrageous."
He noted that the Dow Industrials fell 130 points last Friday but completely recouped losses within two days.
He said the expensive premiums would probably result in lower volume rather than prompt option selling near-term.
"You've obviously got a favorable reaction to that (Greenspan's remarks), but I think at this juncture that's factored in," he said. "I think you're going to see some back-and-forth action."
A brokerage firm trader said the bulk of major quarterly earnings results had already come out, and a seasonal lull might set in for now.
He expected traders to feel more inclined to use spread strategies to manage time decay.
